item.title: Congress Debates Legislative Solutions for Rising AI Data Center Electricity Costs
item.description:
Congress Debates Legislative Solutions for Rising AI Data Center Electricity Costs

Congress is scrambling to address voter concerns over the impact of AI data centers on residential electricity rates as lawmakers debate new legislative measures. With the data center industry rapidly expanding, regional utilities are building tens to hundreds of millions of dollars in new infrastructure, raising questions about how much of these costs will be passed on to everyday utility customers.

⚖️ Legislative Initiatives

Several data center and AI-related bills are moving through Congress. The primary competing measures include:

Bill Name Sponsor / Promoter Key Provisions & Status
Ratepayer Protection Act Sponsored by Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted Would have state utilities consider holding “large-load” customers responsible for increased costs. Passed the House in September with strong bipartisan support; opposed by Senate Minority Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer.
GRID Savings Act Authored by New Mexico Democrat Sen. Martin Heinrich; promoted by Sen. Chuck Schumer Aimed at protecting ratepayers; described by Schumer as having “more teeth” than the Ratepayer Protection Act because the Ratepayer Protection Act’s protections are voluntary.

⚙️ Rising Infrastructure and Utility Costs

The rapid growth of data centers has significantly impacted regional energy grids and wholesale electricity costs:

  • Overall Ratepayer Impact: PJM, a regional transmission organization serving 13 states and the District of Columbia (including Northern Virginia), has an Independent Market Monitor estimating that data centers have cost their 67 million ratepayers approximately $29 billion over roughly the past two years.
  • State-Level Costs: Maryland customers pay an estimated $168 to $216 more per year on electricity bills primarily due to the data center boom.
  • Infrastructure Demands: Utilities are constructing new power lines, substations, and other grid-connecting infrastructure. Connor Waldoch, co-founder and chief strategy officer at Grid Status, notes, “We’re talking tens to hundreds of millions of dollars [of infrastructure] that are being built by these local utilities.”
  • Cost Recovery: Jeremy L. Slayton, a spokesman for Dominion Energy, which serves Loudoun County, Virginia, stated, “We recover costs for distribution and transmission infrastructure from customers.”

🧩 Challenges in Determining Consumer Impact

Calculating the precise cost passed on to residential ratepayers is difficult due to several variables and a lack of transparency:

  • Local Variables: According to Lucy Qiu, a professor at the School of Public Policy at the University of Maryland, consumer impact depends on utilities’ power-purchasing contracts, retail rates, regulatory decisions, the scale of upgrades, and how utilities share accounting.
  • Lack of Transparency: Ari Peskoe, director of the Harvard Electricity Law Initiative, states that a “single, clean number” for nationwide data center costs is impossible because much of the data regarding what data centers pay is hidden behind non-disclosure agreements (NDAs).
  • Prevalence of NDAs: A study by the University of Mary Washington found that NDAs had been signed in 80% of Virginia localities where there were existing, approved, or proposed data centers.

💡 Political Ramifications

The issue of data center growth and energy costs has also entered political campaigns. Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted is currently in a heated reelection campaign against Democrat Sherrod Brown, who lost his Senate seat in 2024. Brown has made Husted’s past support of data centers in Ohio a major campaign issue.

#AIdatacenters #EnergyPolicy #RatepayerProtection #GridInfrastructure

Source: Data centers

item.title: US urges Europe to tap diesel reserves to lower fuel prices
item.description:
US urges Europe to tap diesel reserves to lower fuel prices

The United States is pressing European governments to release a portion of their strategic diesel reserves in order to ease price pressures and address supply disruptions.

🔍 Overview

  • The American Secretary of Energy, Chris Wright, proposed a coordinated plan to release diesel from European strategic reserves.
  • The proposal targets 120 million barrels of diesel over 180 days.
  • This amount is more than one‑third of the roughly 315 million barrels that EU countries held in reserve in June.
  • US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also supported the measure in a post on X.
  • President Donald Trump indicated he could ask Europe to tap their diesel reserves during a visit to Texas.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Release target: 120 million barrels of diesel.
  • Time frame: 180 days.
  • Share of EU reserves: > 33 % of the 315 million barrels reported in June.
  • Winter timing: The minister said, “It is time to bring the diesel stocks to market in a coordinated manner,” as winter approaches.

🗣️ Political Statements

  • Chris Wright told Fox News, “Europe can also contribute to improving the situation.”
  • Scott Bessent wrote on X, “Our European partners should accelerate the implementation of their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions.”
  • President Donald Trump said in Texas, “We could do that. They have diesel,” indicating he could ask Europe to release reserves.
  • On Thursday, Trump’s tone was described as less forceful.

💡 Why it matters

  • Releasing diesel could help lower fuel prices in the United States and Europe.
  • Coordinated market entry aims to stabilize supply ahead of the winter heating season.
  • The request reflects ongoing tensions over President Trump’s earlier threat to impose an export ban on US diesel.
  • European participation would demonstrate trans‑Atlantic cooperation on energy security.

#Diesel #EnergyPolicy #USEuropeRelations

Source: US government calls on Europe to release part of diesel reserves to lower prices

item.title: California passes bills to force data‑center energy and water disclosures
item.description:
California passes bills to force data‑center energy and water disclosures

California Governor Gavin Newsom signed seven bills on Monday that aim to increase transparency around data centers’ electricity and water consumption.

🔍 Overview

  • Data centers are expanding across the U.S., prompting protests over potential strain on power grids and local water supplies.
  • The new California legislation seeks to give communities better data and more say on how data centers impact electricity bills and water supply.

🧩 Legislative Details

Bill Requirement
SB 886, SB 1168, AB 2383 Direct the California Public Utilities Commission to create separate power rates for data centers to recoup grid‑connection costs
AB 1577 Requires monthly reporting on data centers’ energy consumption
AB 2619, AB 2469 Require water‑use disclosures; AB 2469 also makes operators cover infrastructure‑upgrade costs
SB 887 Removes categorical exemptions from the California Environmental Quality Act, ensuring data centers undergo environmental review

⚙️ Why it matters

  • Without clear data, scientists have found it “extremely frustrating to try to understand basic information,” says Mark Specht, senior manager for the climate and energy program at the Union of Concerned Scientists.
  • The disclosure rules begin next year but still won’t provide a full picture of consumption.
  • Two possible outcomes are outlined: (1) ballooning electricity demand could lead to costly new infrastructure that may be overbuilt if AI demand falls, passing costs to other consumers; (2) spreading fixed grid‑maintenance costs across more customers could lower electricity rates, but this depends on data centers contributing to distribution‑system costs rather than only connecting to high‑voltage transmission.
  • Water‑use data remain opaque; water providers have refused to share usage figures, and current disclosures only apply when seeking permits or business licenses, leaving year‑to‑year usage unclear.

📊 Perspectives

  • “I’m happy [AB 1577] passed,” Specht said, noting the difficulty in researching state offers.
  • “I wouldn’t say definitively that data centers have increased the cost [of electricity],” he added, acknowledging the lack of numbers to demonstrate either increase or potential savings.
  • As data centers’ power needs grow, monitoring their energy and water consumption becomes increasingly important.

#California #DataCenters #EnergyPolicy #WaterUse

Source: Data centers are black boxes, but California wants to change that

item.title: California Governor Signs Laws Regulating AI Data Center Energy and Water Use
item.description:
California Governor Signs Laws Regulating AI Data Center Energy and Water Use

California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed a package of seven bills designed to regulate the utility consumption of AI data centers and prevent them from passing costs onto residents.

⚙️ Key details

The new legislation mandates several operational requirements for data centers:

Requirement Description
Rate Classification The California Public Utilities Commission must introduce a new rate classification for data centers.
Infrastructure Costs Data centers are required to pay for upgrades to local power grids and water systems.
Transparency Proposed data centers must disclose estimated water use, energy efficiency, and drought planning to local governments.
Approval Process Facilities must meet specific energy, water, and fuel consumption requirements to qualify for a streamlined approval process.

💡 Why it matters

Governor Newsom stated that these laws aim to ensure that those profiting from data centers do not do so at the expense of residents. He noted that the regulations address community concerns regarding electricity demand, grid constraints, water use, and pollution. Additionally, the Governor signed a separate executive order last week to accelerate the creation of an AI “kill switch.”

#California #AI #DataCenters #EnergyPolicy #Regulation

Source: California tightens rules on AI data center energy and water use
